subQuestions.questionText:
Select the term in Column B that best matches the description in Column A. Each letter may be used only once.

COLUMN A:
(a) An embryonic plant and its food reserve enclosed in a protective coat.
(b) The structure in a flower that produces pollen.
(c) The collective name for all the male reproductive parts of the plant.
(d) An asexual reproductive process for growing many of the same type of plant.
(e) The structure in a flower that develops into the seed of a flowering plant.
(f) The structure down which the pollen tube grows to reach the ovary of the flower.
(g) The term for the fusion of a male gamete with a female gamete.
(h) A natural genetic condition where a plant has more than two sets of chromosomes that may result in larger fruit.
(i) The female part of the flower that produces a sticky substance for the adherence of pollen grains.
(j) The thin stalk that supports the pollen-producing part of the flower.

COLUMN B:
A Anther  B Pollination  C Filament  D Ovule  E Fertilisation  F Stigma  G Style  H Tissue culture  I Seed  J Stamen  K Polyploidy
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) I — seed
(b) A — anther
(c) J — stamen
(d) H — tissue culture
(e) D — ovule
(f) G — style
(g) E — fertilisation
(h) K — polyploidy
(i) F — stigma
(j) C — filament
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText:
What is the function of the clitoris?
A To enhance sexual pleasure.
B To produce lubricating fluids.
C To secrete hormones.
D To decrease blood flow.
subQuestions.memoText: A — to enhance sexual pleasure (it is highly sensitive, richly supplied with nerve endings).

subQuestions.questionText:
HPV can cause warts on the vagina and cancer of the cervix. Figure 1 shows the female reproductive system with numbered parts (1–4). Which numbered parts on Figure 1 will be affected by HPV?
A 1 and 4
B 1 and 3
C 2 and 3
D 3 and 4
(Refer to Figure 1 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: D — 3 and 4 (the parts representing the cervix and the vagina, per the memo key).

subQuestions.questionText:
Among sexually active females, HPV infection is highest in those aged 20–24 (≈50%). Which option would be the best advice to give to females aged 20–24 to lower the risk of becoming infected with HPV?
A To have an IUD inserted.
B To test regularly for HPV.
C To take oral contraceptive pills.
D To use condoms during sexual intercourse.
subQuestions.memoText: D — using condoms during sexual intercourse reduces transmission of HPV (a barrier method); the other options do not prevent infection.

options.D: To use condoms during sexual intercourse.

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 2 shows the structures that develop in an ovary during a typical 28-day menstrual cycle. What event in the ovary does Process A represent?
A Meiosis
B Fertilisation
C Ovulation
D Implantation
(Refer to Figure 2 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: C — ovulation (the release of the ovum from the Graafian follicle).

subQuestions.questionText:
Which row is correct regarding Structure 2 in Figure 2?
A Graafian follicle — Progesterone
B Graafian follicle — FSH
C Corpus luteum — Progesterone
D Corpus luteum — FSH
(Refer to Figure 2 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: C — Structure 2 is the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone.

subQuestions.questionText:
Consider the numbered events in the menstrual cycle of a healthy woman:
1 Ovulation occurs.
2 FSH is secreted.
3 LH reaches its highest level.
4 Progesterone secretion increases.
Which option shows the correct sequence?
A 2 1 3 4
B 2 3 1 4
C 4 1 3 2
D 4 2 3 1
subQuestions.memoText: B — 2 3 1 4: FSH is secreted, then the LH surge, then ovulation, then rising progesterone from the corpus luteum.

subQuestions.questionText:
Which of the secondary sexual characteristics listed below are all true for females during puberty?
(i) Widening of the hips.
(ii) Pronounced deepening of the voice.
(iii) Development of breasts.
(iv) Growth in underarm and pubic hair.
(v) Increased fat distribution.
A (i), (iii), (iv) and (v)
B (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv)
C (i), (iii) and (v)
D (i), (ii), (iii), (iv) and (v)
subQuestions.memoText: A — (i), (iii), (iv) and (v). Pronounced deepening of the voice (ii) is a male characteristic.

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 3 shows some endocrine glands in the human body, labelled with letters. Fill in the table by writing the correct letter of the endocrine gland next to the hormone it secretes: Adrenalin, Thyroxin, Prolactin.
(Refer to Figure 3 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Adrenalin — D (adrenal gland)
Thyroxin — B (thyroid gland)
Prolactin — A (pituitary gland)
(1 mark each; letters as per the memo key)

subQuestions.questionText: An oversecretion of a certain hormone in childhood causes gigantism. Name the hormone and give the letter (from Figure 3) of the endocrine gland that secretes this hormone.
subQuestions.memoText:
Hormone: growth hormone (GH / HGH / somatotropin) (1).
Letter of endocrine gland: A (the pituitary gland) (1).

subQuestions.questionText:
Two population pyramids represent the South African population in 1980 and in 2022. Comparing them, what can you conclude about:
(a) The change in life expectancy.
(b) The change in birth rate.
(Refer to the population pyramids in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Life expectancy has increased — more people are living into old age (into the 90s age group); it was lower in 1980 (1).
(b) The birth rate has decreased — there are fewer people under the age of 30 (a narrower base); it was higher in 1980 (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest a reason for the change in the birth rate.
subQuestions.memoText: Any one: increased use of contraceptives / better access to family planning; women choosing to have children later or to have fewer children; the higher cost of raising children / cost of living; improved education and empowerment of women; the impact of HIV/AIDS on people of child-bearing age.

subQuestions.questionText:
Which age group, A, B or C in population pyramid 2, provides economic support for the citizens of the other age groups?
(Refer to population pyramid 2 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: B — the economically active / working-age group (roughly 15–64 years).

subQuestions.questionText: The South African population was 28 566 771 in 1980 and 60 048 698 in 2022. Calculate the increase in the South African population from 1980 until 2022. Show all working.
subQuestions.memoText: 60 048 698 − 28 566 771 = 31 481 927 people (working + correct answer). (If calculated as a percentage increase: ÷ 28 566 771 × 100 ≈ 110%.)

subQuestions.questionText:
For each row decide which item(s) relate to the term, using: 1 — only item 1; 2 — only item 2; Both; None.
(a) Term: Sex-linked trait. Item 1: Determined by genes located on autosomes. Item 2: Determined by genes located on gonosomes.
(b) Term: Allele. Item 1: An mRNA molecule. Item 2: A random change in DNA sequence.
(c) Term: Phenotype. Item 1: An organism's observable characteristics. Item 2: The genetic make-up of an individual.
(d) Term: Heterozygous. Item 1: Two variations of a gene present in a genotype. Item 2: The expression of the recessive gene will not be evident.
(e) Term: CRISPR. Item 1: A technique used to make more copies of DNA molecules in a sample. Item 2: A micrograph of all the chromosomes in a cell.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) 2
(b) None
(c) 1
(d) Both
(e) None
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText:
A healthy mature human sperm cell has a tail eight times longer than the oval head and a midpiece slightly longer than the head. Figure 4 shows only the midpiece and tail of a sperm cell. On Figure 4, complete the diagram by drawing in and labelling:
(a) The head, showing the correct proportions for a healthy, mature sperm cell.
(b) The nucleus.
(c) The acrosome.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Oval head drawn and labelled, with the correct proportions — the tail about 8× longer than the head and the head shorter than the midpiece (2).
(b) Nucleus correctly placed (in the head) and labelled (1).
(c) Acrosome correctly placed (in front of / capping the nucleus) and labelled (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Will the nucleus in this sperm cell contain a haploid or a diploid set of chromosomes?
subQuestions.memoText: Haploid.

subQuestions.questionText: Scientists investigated the relationship between sperm midpiece length and swimming speed (Table 1: 1,5 µm → 46 µm/s; 2,5 µm → 55 µm/s; 4,5 µm → 80 µm/s; 6 µm → 95 µm/s). Give the name of the structure in the male reproductive system where sperm is stored and matures.
subQuestions.memoText: The epididymis.

subQuestions.questionText: Give a reason why sperm cells with a larger midpiece are more successful at fertilising an ovum.
subQuestions.memoText: 2 marks: a larger midpiece contains more mitochondria, so more energy (ATP) is released by cellular respiration; this increases swimming speed, so the sperm is more likely to reach and fertilise the ovum first.

subQuestions.questionText: Plot a line graph of the data in Table 1 (sperm midpiece length vs swimming speed).
subQuestions.memoText: Marks (7): heading including both variables e.g. "Graph showing the relationship between sperm midpiece length and swimming speed" (1); x-axis labelled "Length of midpiece" (1); y-axis labelled "Swimming speed" (1); units on both axes (1); correct, even scale on both axes (1); line drawn, not joined to the origin (0;0) (1); all points plotted correctly, e.g. 6 µm at 95 µm/s (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Write a conclusion for the investigation.
subQuestions.memoText: 2 marks: an increase in sperm midpiece length results in an increased swimming speed (the statement must link the two variables). Accept equivalent wordings.

subQuestions.questionText:
Study the diabetes infographic. For each statement decide whether it is A — supported, B — contradicted, or C — neither supported nor contradicted by the information:
(a) A blood sample can be taken from a finger to test glucose levels.
(b) Obesity has increased in both men and women in South Africa since 1980.
(c) There are 14,2 million South African adults with diabetes.
(d) The risk of diabetes decreases over the age of 45 years.
(e) Diabetes is the leading cause of death in South Africa.
(Refer to the infographic in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) A
(b) A
(c) B
(d) B
(e) C
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText: Diabetes is characterised by high blood glucose levels, and insulin lowers blood glucose. Describe TWO ways in which insulin functions to lower blood glucose levels.
subQuestions.memoText: Two ways (2 marks each): insulin targets body cells to increase glucose uptake by making the cell membranes more permeable to glucose / opening glucose channels, so glucose is used in cellular respiration; insulin targets the liver (and muscle) cells to convert excess blood glucose into glycogen for storage.

subQuestions.questionText: Human insulin can be made using recombinant DNA technology (Figure 5). What is meant by the term transgenic bacterium in this example?
subQuestions.memoText: 2 marks: a bacterium that contains a foreign gene / DNA from another organism (the human insulin gene) that has been introduced / inserted into it.

subQuestions.questionText:
State the role of the following enzymes in the process shown in Figure 5:
(a) Restriction enzyme
(b) Ligase enzyme
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Cuts the DNA — cuts the insulin gene out of the human genome and cuts open the plasmid DNA (1).
(b) Joins / inserts the insulin gene into the plasmid DNA (seals the sugar-phosphate backbone) (1).

subQuestions.questionText: On Figure 5, place an X at the point in the production process where DNA ligase would function.
subQuestions.memoText: X placed at the point where the insulin gene is being joined into the cut plasmid — anywhere between the sticky ends on the recombinant plasmid (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Experiments in producing transgenic organisms could be unsuccessful (e.g. the wrong proteins are produced). Explain ONE reason why it is important that scientists report the results of any failed experiments.
subQuestions.memoText: One reason explained (2 marks): reporting failures saves other scientists time and money by preventing the same work being repeated; it allows methods to be compared, revised and improved so errors are corrected; scientists learn from the mistakes made and can build on them.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain an advantage of producing insulin using recombinant DNA technology.
subQuestions.memoText: One advantage explained (2 marks): bacteria reproduce very rapidly, so large quantities of insulin can be produced quickly and cheaply; the insulin is human insulin, so it causes fewer allergic side effects than animal insulin; it is more ethical — no animals are farmed or harmed, and it does not clash with religious or cultural practices.

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 6 shows the four cells produced at the end of telophase II of meiosis. Give ONE piece of evidence visible in the cells that shows that meiosis has taken place.
(Refer to Figure 6 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: Any one: all the chromosomes are single-stranded; there are no homologous / paired chromosomes in the cells; the cells are genetically different from one another; crossing over is visible (recombinant chromosomes); four haploid daughter cells (gametes) have been produced.

subQuestions.questionText: Label a centromere on any cell in Figure 6.
subQuestions.memoText: Any centromere correctly identified and labelled on a chromosome (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Explain ONE reason why meiosis is important in sexual reproduction.
subQuestions.memoText: One reason explained (2 marks): meiosis introduces genetic variation through crossing over and independent assortment, giving offspring a better chance of surviving environmental change; OR it halves the chromosome number to form haploid gametes, so that the diploid number is restored (and kept constant) at fertilisation.

subQuestions.questionText: Draw a diagram to represent the parent cell at the end of prophase I that gave rise to the four cells seen in Figure 6. The chromosome number must be correct and the chromosomes clearly visible. No heading is required.
subQuestions.memoText: Marks (5): 4 chromosomes drawn in one cell (1); chromosomes shown double-stranded (each with two chromatids) (1); 2 long and 2 shorter chromosomes shown (1); the chromosomes arranged as two homologous pairs (1); an indication of crossing over / recombination on one homologous pair (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Watson and Crick's first DNA model (Figure 7) was incorrect; using data from Rosalind Franklin's X-ray crystallography photos (obtained via Maurice Wilkins without her awareness) they corrected it and published in Nature in 1953, and Watson, Crick and Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in 1962 after Franklin's death. Give the term for the single unit of a nucleic acid that consists of a sugar molecule, a base and a phosphate molecule.
subQuestions.memoText: Nucleotide.

subQuestions.questionText:
There are four nitrogenous bases in DNA. Provide the name of the base that is complementary to:
(a) Thymine
(b) Guanine
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Adenine (1).
(b) Cytosine (1).

subQuestions.questionText:
Compare TWO ways in which Watson and Crick's incorrect model in Figure 7 differs from the accepted model of the structure of DNA.
(Refer to Figure 7 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: First two comparative differences (2 marks each). Examples: the accepted model has hydrogen bonds joining the strands, the incorrect model had magnesium bonds; the accepted model has the bases on the inside of the double helix, the incorrect model had them facing outwards; the accepted model has bonds between the nitrogenous bases, the incorrect model had bonds between the phosphates; the accepted model is a helix while the incorrect model was flat; the accepted model has antiparallel strands while the incorrect model had parallel strands.

subQuestions.questionText: Do you consider the use of Franklin's crystallography photos by Watson and Crick to be ethical? Explain your answer.
subQuestions.memoText: A reasoned answer (2 marks). NO: they viewed her research without her knowledge or permission; only after seeing her work could they correct their model; they did not credit her in their publication; it was her intellectual property. OR YES: Wilkins was Franklin's colleague also working on DNA; it led to a ground-breaking discovery for the benefit of humanity and opened new fields of research; one could argue there is no private ownership of scientific data and that sharing enabled collaboration.

subQuestions.questionText: Construct a flow diagram to show the process of DNA replication.
subQuestions.memoText:
Heading + correct sequence + 4 correct facts (6 marks):
1. The DNA helix unwinds (helicase).
2. The hydrogen bonds between the two strands break / the strands unzip.
3. Free nucleotides pair with the exposed bases by complementary base pairing (A–T, G–C).
4. DNA polymerase joins the nucleotides, forming the sugar-phosphate backbone of each new strand.
5. The two new double helices rewind.
(Correct sequence = steps 1, 2 and 3 in order.)

subQuestions.questionText: Figure 8 shows a stage in protein synthesis (a ribosome on mRNA with tRNAs bringing amino acids; parts labelled W and X, and positions 3, 4 and 5 on the mRNA). Name the stage of protein synthesis shown in Figure 8.
subQuestions.memoText: Translation.

subQuestions.questionText:
Give the letter that represents:
(a) A section of the protein molecule being constructed
(b) mRNA
(Refer to Figure 8 in the question paper.)
What is the role of tRNA in protein synthesis?
subQuestions.memoText: 2 marks: tRNA carries specific amino acids to the mRNA on the ribosome; its anticodon pairs with the complementary mRNA codon, placing the amino acids in the correct order so that peptide bonds can form to build the protein.

subQuestions.questionText:
Name the bond that forms between parts numbered 4 and 5 (two adjacent amino acids).
(Refer to Figure 8 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: Peptide bond.

subQuestions.questionText:
The table lists mRNA codons and their amino acids: UGC → Cys; ACG → Thr; AGA → Arg; UCU → Ser; UAC → Tyr; GCA → Ala; CGU → Arg. Using the table, work out which amino acids are coded for by numbers 3, 4 and 5 in Figure 8.
(Refer to Figure 8 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
3: Arg
4: Ser
5: Thr
(1 mark each; based on the codons shown at positions 3, 4 and 5 in the figure)

subQuestions.questionText: The Human Genome Project was a large international collaboration to sequence the human genome, with all data made publicly available soon after analysis. State ONE way in which the Human Genome Project has had a positive impact on society.
subQuestions.memoText: Any one: identifies genes that influence the risk of human disease; improves diagnosis and diagnostic tests; allows earlier detection of genetic predispositions; improves drug design (pharmacogenomics), gene therapy and molecular medicine; aids the study of human evolution and migration; established an open approach to data sharing; drove the development of better sequencing technology.

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest why it is beneficial that the human genome data was released shortly after it was analysed.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): it was a collaborative effort by many scientists, so data had to be shared; it prevents duplication of work; it speeds up research so that no time is wasted; it allows further research (e.g. into inherited diseases) to begin immediately.

subQuestions.questionText: Leigh syndrome is a severe neurological disorder, usually appearing in the first year of life, caused by mutations in any of more than 75 genes located in the nuclear or mitochondrial DNA, most commonly inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. What is a mutation?
subQuestions.memoText: A change (rearrangement, deletion, addition, substitution or translocation) in the DNA sequence / structure of a gene or chromosome — a change in the order of nitrogenous bases / genetic make-up of an individual.

subQuestions.questionText:
Which option is the most correct description of the term loci? Circle the letter of your choice.
A Two or more versions of a DNA sequence for a gene.
B The position or place of a gene on a chromosome.
C Multiple genes that influence the expression of a characteristic.
subQuestions.memoText: B — the position / place of a gene on a chromosome.

options.A: Two or more versions of a DNA sequence for a gene.
options.B: The position or place of a gene on a chromosome.
options.C: Multiple genes that influence the expression of a characteristic.

subQuestions.questionText: Why are traits coded for by mtDNA not passed on to children by their fathers?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): at fertilisation only the head of the sperm (containing the nuclear DNA) enters the ovum; the midpiece of the sperm, which contains its mitochondria, is left outside / excluded; so only the mother's mitochondria (and mtDNA) are present in the zygote.

subQuestions.questionText:
A pedigree chart shows the autosomal recessive inheritance of Leigh syndrome. Individual 3 (in circle P) is a deceased affected male, the child of unaffected parents 1 and 2.
(a) List THREE facts that can be determined from the symbol for individual 3 in circle P.
(b) By means of a genetic diagram, show how individuals 1 and 2 passed on Leigh syndrome to some of their children. Include: parental genotypes; a genetic cross or Punnett diagram; and the probable genotypic and phenotypic ratios of the offspring. Key: B = unaffected, b = mutation causing Leigh syndrome.
(Refer to the pedigree chart in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Any 3 (1 mark each): individual 3 is male; is affected / has Leigh syndrome; is homozygous recessive (bb); is deceased.
(b) Parental genotypes: Bb × Bb (both carriers) (1); Punnett square with gametes B, b on each axis giving BB, Bb, Bb, bb (2); genotypic ratio 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb (1); phenotypic ratio 3 unaffected : 1 affected (Leigh syndrome) (2). (If parental genotypes are wrong, max 2 — carry the error forward for the cross only.)

subQuestions.questionText:
South African abalone (perlemoen) are endemic marine snails whose wild populations have crashed due to poaching. Table 2 gives facts about abalone reproduction: eggs and sperm are released into the water (spawning); immature abalone (2,5 cm shell) release ~10 000 eggs, mature abalone (20 cm shell) over 10 million; fertilised eggs hatch into larvae 1 day after fertilisation; larval mortality possibly exceeds 98%; wild abalone reach sexual maturity at 7 years; fewer than 1 in 10 000 reach maturity. Which option is TRUE regarding the reproductive strategies of abalone? Write only the correct letter.
A External fertilisation — Viviparous
B Internal fertilisation — Ovoviviparous
C External fertilisation — Oviparous
subQuestions.memoText: C — external fertilisation (gametes released into the water) and oviparous (eggs laid; development outside the body).

subQuestions.questionText: Explain how the ability to produce between 10 000 and 10 million eggs improves the reproductive success of abalone.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): producing huge numbers of eggs increases the chance that some will be fertilised, so more offspring are produced; many gametes are carried away by water currents and never fertilised; many eggs and larvae are eaten by predators — a large egg number compensates for these heavy losses.

subQuestions.questionText:
(a) Are abalone an example of an r-strategist or a k-strategist species? Provide two supporting facts from the data in Table 2.
(b) Sketch a simple graph of a survivorship curve for abalone. (No heading required.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) r-strategist (1) + any 2 facts (2): very high larval mortality (~98%); very large number of eggs produced (10 000–10 million); very low survival rate (fewer than 1 in 10 000 reach maturity).
(b) Graph (3): x-axis labelled (age); y-axis labelled (percentage / number of offspring surviving); a Type III curve — a steep drop in survivors early in life, then levelling off (1 mark each).

subQuestions.questionText: Poachers target the larger 20 cm abalone because they are more profitable. Explain the impact that this activity will have on abalone populations in the future.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 (3 marks): the number of large, mature abalone in the wild decreases; far fewer eggs are released (10 000 from a small abalone vs over 10 million from a large one), so the natality rate falls and the population size decreases; once the 20 cm abalone are gone, poachers target the immature abalone; the species is at risk of not being able to maintain its population / of extinction.

subQuestions.questionText: The Barcode of Wildlife Project (BWP) is creating a DNA reference library of the world's most threatened species (including abalone), for accurate identification, border inspections and courtroom prosecutions. Provide TWO ways in which data from the Barcode of Wildlife Project can be used.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): accurate identification of threatened species; use in courtroom prosecutions to identify poached specimens; use at border inspections to identify illegally traded / exported specimens.

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest a reason why it may be difficult to obtain DNA samples from abalone.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): abalone are hard to locate — you must know where they occur along the coastline, and they hide between rocks; sampling is time-consuming and requires scuba diving with special equipment and skills; boats, trained staff and good weather are needed, making it expensive; wild numbers are very low due to poaching, so they are difficult to find.

subQuestions.questionText:
Abalone confiscated from poachers were DNA-profiled against three library species (A, B, C). All the bands of the unknown specimen line up with those of species C.
(a) To which species does the unknown specimen most likely belong? Give a reason for your answer.
(b) Why is non-coding DNA used in DNA profiling?
(c) Describe ONE measure that the South African authorities can put in place to reduce abalone poaching.
(Refer to the DNA profiles in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Species C (1) — all of its DNA bands match / align with those of the unknown specimen (1).
(b) Non-coding DNA is highly variable between individuals, so it gives a unique profile for every individual (1).
(c) Any one, described (2): stricter checks at border crossings; heavier penalties (fines / jail) to deter poachers; more patrols and guarding of coastline hotspots; a dedicated, trained law-enforcement unit targeting poaching hotspots; creating alternative job opportunities for coastal communities.

subQuestions.questionText: A research team bred a hybrid between two varieties of blacklip abalone (Haliotis rubra) — one with high-quality, high-yield meat and one with a fast growth rate — and the hybrid showed all these traits. Key criteria: (1) establish a closed population; (2) use genetically diverse breeding individuals; (3) all breeding individuals healthy. Explain the meaning of the term hybrid.
subQuestions.memoText: 2 marks: the offspring of two genetically dissimilar parents (different breeds or varieties); or the heterozygous offspring produced by crossing two homozygous parents.

subQuestions.questionText: State two phenotypic traits that were selected for in the breeding programme.
subQuestions.memoText: High-quality / large amount of meat (1); fast growth rate (1).

subQuestions.questionText:
Justify why each criterion listed in the breeding programme is scientifically important:
Criterion 1: establish a closed population.
Criterion 2: breeding individuals are genetically diverse.
Criterion 3: all breeding individuals are healthy.
subQuestions.memoText:
Each criterion — 2 marks:
Criterion 1: a closed population prevents migration in or out, so no foreign DNA is introduced, the genetic outcome is known and controlled, and hybrids cannot escape into wild populations.
Criterion 2: genetically diverse parents give greater variation in the offspring and prevent inbreeding, which would raise the frequency of harmful traits.
Criterion 3: healthy breeding stock improves reproductive success and produces healthy offspring, prevents the spread of disease, maintains ethical standards and maximises yield / profit.

subQuestions.questionText:
An abalone farm investigated the effect of population density on abalone growth: abalone were kept at high, medium and low densities in tanks at 18 °C, fed seaweed, and the growth in shell length and mass of seaweed consumed were measured (Figure 10). Identify:
(a) The independent variable.
(b) One controlled variable.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) The density of the abalone population (1).
(b) Any one: water temperature (18 °C) / type of diet (seaweed) / water quality (1).

subQuestions.questionText:
What was the growth in shell length when the abalone were placed in medium-density water tanks?
(Refer to Figure 10 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: About 0,04 mm/day (read from the graph) (2 marks).

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to your understanding of density-dependent factors to explain the differences in the growth of shell length at:
(a) High density.
(b) Low density.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) High density (2 marks): competition for food and space is high, with more waste accumulation and greater spread of parasites/disease, so shell-length growth is low (≈0,03 mm/day).
(b) Low density (2 marks): there is less competition, more food and space per abalone and less waste build-up, so shell-length growth is higher (≈0,09 mm/day).

subQuestions.questionText: The killer whale (Orcinus orca), the largest dolphin, is an apex predator found in all oceans, with a diverse diet and complex matriarchal 'pods' of 2–15 (occasionally up to 100) individuals whose hunting techniques and vocalisations are passed across generations. What is meant by the term predator?
subQuestions.memoText: 2 marks: an organism that catches, kills and eats another animal (its prey).

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to Figure 12 (a marine food web).
(a) Draw a food chain from the food web that consists of five organisms. (Diagrams of organisms are not required.)
(b) Explain why ecosystems may not have many food chains with four or more trophic levels.
(Refer to Figure 12 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Any valid 5-organism chain from the web (3 marks): e.g. plankton → small fish → squid → large fish → killer whale, or algae → small fish → large fish → great white shark → killer whale. Must start with a producer (plankton/algae), contain 5 organisms ending with the killer whale, and have arrows pointing in the direction of energy flow.
(b) 2 marks: energy is lost at each trophic level (in life processes, movement, heat and waste), so only about 10% passes to the next level — after several levels too little energy remains to support another trophic level.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain TWO ways in which the social organisation of killer whale pods improves their chances of survival.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 explained (2 marks each): the pod (2–15 individuals) gives safety in numbers; co-operative hunting with communication makes hunting more successful and allows larger prey to be caught, providing more food; more individuals increases the chance of locating prey; older whales teach hunting techniques to younger whales, so knowledge is passed on.

subQuestions.questionText: State TWO similarities between the social structure of killer whales and wild dogs.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): both live in groups with a large number of individuals; both have a dominant female / females that lead; both show co-operative hunting; both care for the young communally; both communicate (vocal behaviour) between members.

subQuestions.questionText: Killer whales are placental mammals; the foetus and mother are connected by an umbilical cord containing two arteries and two veins. Give TWO functions of the placenta in mammals.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): supplies nutrients from the mother's blood to the foetus; removes metabolic wastes (excretion) from the foetus; allows gaseous exchange (oxygen to the foetus, carbon dioxide away); acts as a barrier / microfilter against many pathogens; allows maternal antibodies through (passive immunity); secretes hormones (oestrogen and progesterone) to maintain pregnancy.

subQuestions.questionText: Clearly describe the position of the umbilical cord in mammals.
subQuestions.memoText: 2 marks: it runs between (connects) the foetus and the placenta, attaching the foetus to the placenta on the wall of the uterus.

subQuestions.questionText: The Shark Spotters organisation scans the ocean with binoculars from vantage points and records shark sightings and warns swimmers. In 2015 a pair of great-white-hunting killer whales was recorded in False Bay. Figure 13 shows the number of great white shark sightings in False Bay since 2004, with the point when killer whales were first seen marked. From the graph, what effect did the presence of the killer whales in the False Bay area have on the sightings of great white sharks?
subQuestions.memoText: The number of great white shark sightings decreased (after the killer whales appeared).

subQuestions.questionText: State the type of competition that exists between killer whales and great white sharks. Give a reason for your answer.
subQuestions.memoText: Interspecific competition (1) — killer whales and great white sharks are different species (competing for the same prey, e.g. seals) (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Why are 'the number of sightings' of great white sharks by Shark Spotters not a reliable sampling method of the actual great white shark population of False Bay?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 (3 marks): it is not a direct count / census — not every individual is counted; there is no random sampling; sharks are not tagged, so the same shark can be counted more than once; identification is subjective / biased; sightings depend on water and light conditions and only large sharks near the shore can be seen (deep-water sharks are missed); no statistical formula is applied to produce an estimate; it is not a closed population.

subQuestions.questionText: Provide TWO reasons why the work of the Shark Spotters organisation is of value.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): it warns and alerts swimmers of the presence of sharks, improving public safety and helping prevent shark attacks; it provides scientists, tourists, surfers and fishermen with valuable data on shark locations; it raises awareness about sharks; it provides employment.

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 14 shows ecological succession (community change over time) in a nature reserve, beginning on bare rock. Is Figure 14 an example of primary or secondary succession? Give a reason for your answer.
(Refer to Figure 14 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: Primary succession (1) — the pioneers become established on bare rock with no soil present initially / no plants existed there before (1).

subQuestions.questionText:
(a) From the numbered list — 1 All organisms are of the same species; 2 Organisms are of many different species; 3 Includes only the abiotic factors; 4 Organisms live in different biomes; 5 Organisms live in the same area — select the TWO most correct items that apply to the term 'community'. Write only the numbers.
(b) Provide the letter (A, B or C) from Figure 14 that represents: (i) Climax community; (ii) Pioneer community.
(c) Construct a table to compare any TWO differences between climax and pioneer communities.
(Refer to Figure 14 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) 2 and 5 (2).
(b) (i) C (1); (ii) A (1).
(c) Table with a heading and correct construction + 2 comparative differences (4). Examples:
Pioneer community | Climax community
Small-sized, fast-growing, short-lived species | Large-sized, slow-growing, long-lived species
First community to appear; establishes in 1–2 years | Last community to appear; takes 100+ years
Poor competitors, tolerant of extreme conditions | Good competitors, need more fertile soil
Low biodiversity | High biodiversity

subQuestions.questionText: A biologist used mark-recapture to estimate a field mouse population. First capture: 34 mice tagged and released. Two weeks later: 52 mice captured, of which 13 were tagged. Calculate the estimated population size of field mice in the nature reserve. Show all working.
subQuestions.memoText: Population = (first marked × second sample) ÷ number recaptured marked = (34 × 52) ÷ 13 = 136 mice (3 marks — working + answer).

subQuestions.questionText: Give TWO precautions that the biologist must take to improve the accuracy of the mark-recapture method.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): allow enough time for the marked mice to mix freely back into the population before the second capture; ensure the marks stay on and remain visible for the whole investigation; keep the time between captures short so births, deaths and migration are minimal (a closed population); ensure the mark does not harm the mice, hinder their movement or make them more visible to predators.
